message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This study is built on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households across three deliberately mixed wards, so the projections are based on how Thornbury residents actually behave, not national averages. We measured participation and tonnage weekly, by housing type, and the results are encouraging: strong participation, consistent yields and 81% of residents rating the service good or very good. Crucially, participation held up across houses and flats, which means we can roll out a single, simple service across the district rather than designing separate arrangements. The financial analysis is complete and transparent. Every cost line is shown, from vehicles to liners, and the disposal saving uses our actual incineration cost and Brookfield's quoted gate fee, giving a net cost of about £490,000 that is fully covered by the provisional new-burdens allocation. Treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away. The timetable works back from the vehicle lead time. I am confident the Council can approve this roll-out knowing it is evidence-based and fully funded.
</author>

<document>
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.
</document>
response:
The pilot is useful, and the cost table adds up. But the study's two main conclusions don't hold. The pilot shows flats participating at a third of the rate of houses, not "broadly similar". And the treatment and funding position depends on a plant that can take only part of the projected tonnage. Once those are corrected, the service is no longer shown to be fully funded.

## What holds up

- **Table 1 arithmetic.** Houses 2,112 / 3,200 = 66%, flats 168 / 800 = 21%, all 2,280 / 4,000 = 57%. The weighted average yield is about 1.86 kg, which rounds to 1.9 ✓.
- **Table 2 arithmetic.**
  - Vehicles: £990,000 / 7 = £141,400 ✓
  - Crews: 12 × £34,000 = £408,000 ✓
  - Total: £733,400 ✓
- **Disposal saving per tonne.** £112 − £38 = £74 ✓. 3,290 t × £74 ≈ £243,000 ✓.
- **Other pilot evidence.** Contamination measured at the plant, falling missed collections and resident feedback are genuine positives.

## Main problems

**1. Flats did not participate at a similar rate to houses.** Houses were at 66% and flats at 21%. The text says participation "held up across houses and flats", and the case for a uniform service rests on that. The pilot shows the opposite.

Flats probably need their own approach: communal bins, bin-store placement, and engagement with managing agents. Roughly 10,400 of the district's households are flats, so this is a significant gap, not a detail.

**2. The projection uses a participation rate the pilot didn't produce.** Section 3 applies 64%, but the pilot achieved 57% overall. The pilot also had exactly the district's mix of 20% flats, so there's no reason to adjust upward. Projecting each housing type separately:

| | Households | Participation | kg/week | Tonnes/year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | ≈ 2,710 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | ≈ 160 |
| **Total** | **52,000** | | | **≈ 2,870** |

That is about 2,870 tonnes, not 3,290. The disposal saving falls to about £212,000 even if every tonne goes to Brookfield.

**3. Brookfield can take only 1,800 tonnes until 2029.** The study notes this limit but never applies it. That leaves about 1,070 tonnes a year without local capacity. The saving is only £74 a tonne for the first 1,800 tonnes, which is about £133,000. The rest has to go to the plant 46 miles away, at an unknown gate fee plus haulage costs, or the saving disappears.

Incinerating separately collected food waste would probably also undermine compliance with the duty this service exists to meet. The claim that "treatment is local" is true only for part of the waste.

**4. The service is not shown to be fully funded.**

| | £ per year |
|---|---|
| Costs as shown | 733,400 |
| Saving, best case: all 2,870 t at £74 | −212,000 |
| Saving, if the excess earns nothing: 1,800 t only | −133,000 |
| **Net cost** | **≈ 521,000 to 600,000** |

Even before the missing costs in point 5, the net cost sits at or above the £520,000 provisional allocation. That allocation is also provisional. The study should state its basis, how confident the Council is in it, and how many years it covers.

**5. Several cost lines appear to be missing.** The author describes the table as including "every cost line". These items are absent or unclear:

- **Staff costs.** Is £34,000 per operative salary only, or does it include National Insurance and pension? Is there cover for holidays and sickness?
- **Spare capacity.** There is no spare vehicle for breakdowns or servicing.
- **Overheads.** Supervision and management, depot space, and the dedicated phone line and web page described in Section 6.
- **One-off costs.** Delivering caddies to 52,000 households, recruitment, and training.
- **Haulage.** Transport for the roughly 1,070 tonnes going beyond Brookfield.
- **Round capacity.** Six vehicles serving every household weekly works out to about 1,700 properties per vehicle per day. Is that feasible on these rounds, with tipping trips 14 miles away and some loads travelling 46 miles?

There may also be an upside not counted: lighter residual-waste rounds could save money.

**6. The timetable has no slack.** Vehicles are ordered in December and delivered in March. Crews are trained on them in March, caddies go to 52,000 households in March, and collections start on 5 April. Vehicle lead times often slip, and any delay at one stage pushes back the launch.

The statutory date also needs checking. My understanding is that English councils' duty to collect food waste applies from 31 March 2026, unless a council has a transitional arrangement. If that applies to Thornbury, an April 2027 start is already after the deadline. The study should state the Council's compliance position.

## Smaller points

- **Satisfaction.** "81% of surveyed pilot households" needs a response rate and who was surveyed. If mainly participants responded, the figure overstates satisfaction across all households.
- **Pilot selection and duration.** The pilot wards were chosen, not randomly selected, and six months may include some early enthusiasm that fades. Neither point is serious, but both are worth stating.

## On the author's description

- **Participation "held up across houses and flats".** The pilot data show the reverse.
- **Treatment "is local".** This is true for 1,800 of roughly 2,870 tonnes.
- **"Every cost line is shown".** Several lines are missing.
- **"Fully covered by the new-burdens allocation".** Not shown once tonnage and capacity are corrected.
- **The timetable "works back from the vehicle lead time".** It does, but with no buffer.

## Suggested changes before Cabinet

1. Project tonnage separately for houses and flats using the pilot rates, which gives about 2,870 t.
2. Model treatment explicitly: 1,800 t at Brookfield, the remainder at the 46-mile plant with a quoted gate fee and haulage cost.
3. Complete the cost table, including on-costs, cover, a spare vehicle, overheads and one-off costs, and show net cost against the allocation with a sensitivity range.
4. Design a separate approach for flats.
5. Add contingency to the timetable and state the statutory compliance position.

The roll-out may well still be the right decision, and for the Council it is largely required anyway. But Cabinet should approve it knowing it probably needs funding beyond the provisional allocation and a separate approach for flats.
